blocks.prompt: 10 If \(\frac{b + c - a}{a}, \frac{c + a - b}{b}, \frac{a + b - c}{c}\) are in A.P., show that \(a, b, c\) are in H.P.
blocks.explanation:
A proof. We must reach "\(\frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{b}, \frac{1}{c}\) are in A.P."
Trick: adding the same number to every term of an A.P. keeps it an A.P.
Plan: add 2 to each term, take \(a + b + c\) common, divide it out.
steps:
Given: \(\frac{b + c - a}{a}, \frac{c + a - b}{b}, \frac{a + b - c}{c}\) are in A.P.
To prove: \(a, b, c\) are in H.P.
Method: Adding a constant to all terms, or dividing all terms by a non-zero constant, keeps an A.P. an A.P.

Add 2 to each term
\[\dfrac{b + c - a}{a} + 2 = \dfrac{a + b + c}{a}\]
\[\dfrac{c + a - b}{b} + 2 = \dfrac{a + b + c}{b}\]
\[\dfrac{a + b - c}{c} + 2 = \dfrac{a + b + c}{c}\]
Why: \(2 = \frac{2a}{a}\), and \(b + c - a + 2a = a + b + c\); the same for the others. The common difference does not change.

So these are in A.P.
\[\dfrac{a + b + c}{a}, \; \dfrac{a + b + c}{b}, \; \dfrac{a + b + c}{c}\]
Why: The new terms are the old ones shifted by 2.

Divide by \(a + b + c\)
\[\dfrac{1}{a}, \; \dfrac{1}{b}, \; \dfrac{1}{c} \text{ are in A.P.}\]
Why: Dividing every term by the same non-zero number divides the common difference by it, so the terms stay in A.P. (we take \(a + b + c \ne 0\)).

Conclude
Why: The reciprocals of \(a, b, c\) are in A.P., so \(a, b, c\) are in H.P.

Check with numbers: \(a = 1, b = \frac{1}{2}, c = \frac{1}{3}\) (an H.P.). The terms become \(-\frac{1}{6} \div 1\), \(\frac{5}{6} \div \frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{7}{6} \div \frac{1}{3}\), i.e. \(-\frac{1}{6}, \frac{5}{3}, \frac{7}{2}\): differences \(\frac{11}{6}\) and \(\frac{11}{6}\) \(\checkmark\).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(a, b, c\) are in H.P.
